title: Short Stuff: NATO Alphabet
summary: Short Stuff episode on the NATO phonetic alphabet. Chuck and Josh explain why people spell words aloud over radio and phone calls, since telegrams made spelling unnecessary but radio communication in chaotic or life-and-death situations required clear letter codes. They trace the history: a 1920s telecom-industry alphabet of city names (Amsterdam, Baltimore, etc.), the Army-Navy phonetic alphabet (Able, Baker, etc.) used by the military and British, the 1951 International Air Transport Association (IATA) revisions for civil aviation, and the NATO committee dispute over words like Nectar versus November, which ended with the NATO Military Standing Group adopting the list before the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) signed on. By 1956 civilian and military users converged on the current alphabet. The episode also includes a non-educational side story from Chuck about a stale popcorn complaint at a movie theater.

segments.title: Opening banter and customer service spelling
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the short episode on the phonetic alphabet and Chuck describes spelling his name with word substitutes on customer service calls.

segments.title: Why spell letters: radio and telegrams
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh explain that telegrams made spelling unnecessary, but radio communication, especially in war, needed spelled-out letters to avoid confusion, since listeners cannot see the speaker's lips.

segments.title: 1920s telecom city-name alphabet
segments.summary: The first agreed alphabet came in the 1920s from the International Telecommunications Union and used city names such as Amsterdam, Baltimore, and Casablanca. Josh reads the list, including Gallipoli and Havana.

segments.title: Army Navy phonetic alphabet
segments.summary: The military used the Army Navy phonetic alphabet, starting with Able and Baker, which the British also used with Zebra or Zebra. The hosts read the full list.

segments.title: Chuck's movie theater popcorn story
segments.summary: Chuck recounts a dispute at a Landmark Midtown Cinema over stale popcorn and an employee's rude comment, which the manager did not address before refunding him.

segments.title: 1951 IATA civil aviation revisions
segments.summary: Ten years after the military alphabet, the International Air Transport Association revised words to reduce English-centric choices for civil aviation, swapping Coca for Charlie, Easy for Echo, Fox for Foxtrot, and Item for India, among others. Delta replaced dog in discussion.

segments.title: Alpha spelling
segments.summary: Josh notes that Alpha is spelled Alfa in the alphabet, and Chuck says the earlier version used Alpha because Amsterdam was the only previous A word.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break and a brief promotional line for another show is heard.

segments.title: NATO committee and Nectar versus November
segments.summary: NATO formed a committee to settle changes to words including Nectar and November, which took years of argument. The NATO Military Standing Group adopted the list, and NATO began using it before the International Civil Aviation Organization signed on.

segments.title: Convergence in 1956 and pronunciations
segments.summary: By 1956 civilian and military groups agreed on the current list, with Charlie, Mike, November, Uniform, and X-ray. The hosts note the published pronunciations, such as Oscar and Victor, which they find amusing.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the Short Stuff episode and close with the show's credits and podcast app mention.
